name: Drupal installer
tile_line: Both bugs exploited, no login. First in CISA KEV.
tldr: Drupal's installer, `install.php`, can let someone with no login take over a site. Drupal's 18 Nov fix was incomplete, and both bugs are exploited; the first is in CISA KEV. Block `install.php`, check for a takeover, then update and run `update.php`.
summary: The first bug (CVE-2026-132165, 18 Nov, Highly critical 20 of 25, complex attack) is in CISA KEV; Drupal credits Anthropic's OSS Scanner with finding it and reports attacks from 19 Nov, and a proof of concept posted on GitHub on 20 Nov replaces the main admin account on 11.4.12 after planting a half-finished installer state itself, and shows no code execution. The second (CVE-2026-136716, 25 Nov, 21 of 25, basic attack) is about sites left in an unusual or incomplete install state, production sites included, which stayed open to takeover after the first fix; Drupal gives no date or source for attacks on it. The new fix makes the installer refuse to continue an install that has no session token recorded, and an update hook marks stuck sites as installed, which is why `update.php` must run.

affected.label: Drupal core, not updated
affected.text: Affected: before 10.6.23, 11.0.0 up to 11.3.22, and 11.4.0 up to 11.4.13; 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23 are fixed. Sites that installed only the 18 Nov releases (11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22) are still affected. Drupal 11.2 and below, 10.5 and below, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The command prints your version.

affected.label: An attacker can reach install.php
affected.text: Attacks go through the installer at `/core/install.php`, which stays reachable after installation unless you block it. Drupal says sites that have already secured the installer aren't vulnerable to the second bug. Horizon3 notes this isn't only about internet-facing sites: internal and staging sites count if an attacker can reach them. Drupal's check: each of these URLs on your site should end with `403` or `404`; a `200` means the installer isn't blocked. Also try `/core/install.php/foo` and, following redirects (`curl -IL`), `/install.php`.

affected.label: A setup Drupal calls uncommon
affected.text: Drupal rates both bugs as needing an uncommon setup (`TD:Uncommon`) and doesn't list which. For the second bug it says sites in "unusual or incomplete install states" stayed vulnerable after the first fix, and that you can't tell from the user interface whether yours is one. A related, older hole is public: on Drupal's issue 3455853, a site whose translation import was left pending or failed lets `install.php` run again and replace the admin account. Drupal release manager catch says the first fix closes it "as a by-product". A 2025 report of `install.php` offering to reinstall a finished site, not translation-related, was closed by catch, who said the first fix "should have resolved this issue too". The proof of concept plants a similar unfinished installer state by hand. For the first bug, Drupal says some exploit paths, but not all, are blocked if the web server can't write to or change permissions on `settings.php`; the 18 Nov releases stopped the installer fixing those permissions.

do.label: Block install.php first
do.text: Drupal recommends blocking the installer in the web server, which survives core updates, and says sites that have already secured it aren't vulnerable to the second bug. nginx: add the block below to the HTTPS `server` block; Drupal says to use `^~`, not an exact match (`=`), which on some servers doesn't block `/core/install.php/foo`. Apache: in the virtual host, `<Location "/core/install.php">` with `Require all denied`. Apache without access to the virtual host: Drupal's docs also give an `.htaccess` rule (`<Files "install.php">` with `Require all denied`), but Composer overwrites `.htaccess`, so lines added by hand are lost. Test with `nginx -t` or `apachectl configtest` before reloading, then rerun the check above. Drupal Steward sites with its recommended mitigations are already protected from the known attack paths for both bugs, but should still update.

do.label: Check for a takeover, before update.php
do.text: Drupal's guide says to run its checks before database updates, because the update rewrites the install state they read, and to copy your web server logs somewhere safe now, since some hosts keep them only a few days. The command prints the install state: anything other than `done` means the site is vulnerable now, but `done` doesn't prove it's safe, because a successful attack also sets it. Drupal says any site that left its installer reachable after the first fix may still have been compromised, and a site that was taken over may no longer be in the vulnerable state, so a clean-looking site isn't proof. Check your logs for changes to user 1, the site's first admin account, or made by it; make sure user 1's email address is one you control, and consider resetting its password. The public proof of concept replaces user 1's name, email and password, so the old admin password stops working; content is left in place. In your web logs since 18 Nov 2026, an installed site answers every installer request with `200`, so that alone isn't a sign; Drupal says to look into `POST` requests to `/core/install.php` that return `302` or `303`, much larger responses, and many installer requests from one address within minutes. If you find signs, follow Drupal's "Your Drupal site got hacked" guide and assume the attacker had admin rights and may have run code on the server. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies must also do CISA's forensic triage.

do.label: Update Drupal
do.text: 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 (25 Nov 2026), then run `update.php` once you've done the checks above. Drupal says the code update closes the hole right away, and the update hook then repairs sites stuck in the vulnerable state. The 25 Nov release notes say they also fix the theme registry bug the 18 Nov releases introduced ("Theme hook field not found", seen with Search API), and that a Symfony security update from the same day isn't included, so update Symfony too. 11.3 and 10.6 get security fixes only until Drupal 11.5.0 comes out in December 2026; on 11.2, 10.5 or older, move to a supported line.

do.label: Why it's Patch now
do.text: Drupal rates the exploitable setups as uncommon (`TD:Uncommon`) but doesn't list them, and says the user interface doesn't show whether a site is in the vulnerable state, so you can't rule your site out. `install.php` stays reachable unless you block it, attacks on live sites are reported for both bugs, and the first is in CISA KEV. A related, older hole in the installer was already being probed: on 28 Oct 2025 someone on Drupal's issue 3455853 reported automated requests trying to exploit it. The workaround is one web server rule.

changes.text: Drupal's 18 Nov fix was incomplete: a second bug (CVE-2026-136716, SA-CORE-2026-019) is also exploited. The fix is now 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 plus running `update.php`, after Drupal's checks for a takeover, which the update would disturb.
